newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Agencies help some Rwandan refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Agencies help some Rwandan refugees in Zaire.

text.p: Aid agencies helped some of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees emerging from hiding in Zaire on Tuesday but fell far short of the pace needed to meet a rebel deadline for them to be repatriated in 60 days.

The rebels failed the first test on Monday of rebel leader Laurent Kabila's promise on Sunday of free access to refugees when an aid convoy was turned back at a checkpoint at Biaro, 41 km (25 miles) south of the northeastern capital of Kisangani.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said out of 21 sick refugees driven out of Biaro camp on Monday, one had died and two were having limbs amputated on Tuesday because of gangrenous wounds.

"It seems today the (rebel) alliance is requiring escorts and limiting the number of aid vehicles allowed south of Kisangani," said UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg. "These are not the arrangements which we agreed with the governor last night."

Three trucks out of 11 allowed to reach Biaro on Tuesday unloaded food and other aid and picked up 160 unaccompanied children and brought them back to Kisangani, from where they will be repatriated by air on Wednesday, UNHCR officials said.

"The other refugees in Biaro were very anxious to leave but with only three trucks we could only take 160," said UNHCR spokeswoman Antonella Gesulfo, adding nothing was known for sure about a train rebels said would pick up refugees on Tuesday.
She said a plane flew to the northwestern Rwandan town of Gisenyi with 21 Rwandan refugees including nine children.
"It is still too early to give a general judgement about cooperation (with the rebels). It is mainly a question of exchanging information and coordination," Gesulfo added.
Some 85,000 Hutu refugees from Kasese and Biaro camps south of Kisangani were among up to 100,000 south of Kisangani missing since aid agencies were barred from camps by rebels last week.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
An outbreak of cholera was cited by rebels as the reason for delaying a U.N. airlift earlier this month of the refugees.
Kabila demanded on Sunday that aid agencies repatriate all the remaining Rwandan refugees in Zaire within 60 days.
Aid workers say it is impossible to repatriate all 100,000 south of Kisangani and another 250,000 Rwandan refugees who are unaccounted for in Zaire even with full rebel cooperation.
In Luxembourg, Emma Bonino, the EU Commissioner responsible for humanitarian aid, accused rebels of a deliberate drive to wipe out refugees because of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

"There can be little doubt that human rights abuses are being perpetrated against refugees," she told a news conference. "I strongly believe that this is the result of a deliberate strategy to get rid of these people."

She spoke after the U.N. refugee agency said in Geneva it had "increasingly shocking reports" of killings of refugees around Kisangani and other areas of eastern Zaire held by the Tutsi-dominated rebels and demanded a full investigation.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said it was relatively satisfied by access to refugees allowed by rebels on Tuesday.

A WFP spokeswoman said five WFP food trucks were permitted to drive south of Kisangani and the city's large international airport was opened to aid flights on Tuesday for the first time since it fell to rebels in March and mines were cleared.

Before they were turned back on Monday, aid workers and journalists saw some 5,000 Hutu refugees emerge from the forests and return to Biaro, which they said they fled last week after being attacked by villagers and the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
Aid workers said up to 10,000 arrived at Biaro by Tuesday.
Dozens of those emerging from the forest on Monday were very ill -- many with cholera, doctors said -- and others bore horrific wounds from the attacks that sparked their exodus.

Rebel authorities have denied attacking camps at Kasese and Biaro last week. They said rebels intervened and were ambushed by Rwandan militiamen among the refugees only after villagers attacked camps to avenge the killing of six Zairean civilians.
The Hutu refugees at Biaro appeared terrified. One priority for aid workers was to bury the dozens of bodies in the camps.
Refugees reported seeing hundreds of bodies in the forest.
